To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

castration leads to a decrease of specific protein synthesis in isolated tissue, and androgen therapy with testosterone or dihydro-testosterone, but not 3alpha-androstane-diol, restores the capability of the tissue to synthesize these proteins.

androgen deprivation decreases the synthesis in vivo of specific proteins by the epithelium of seminal vesicles, and that androgens are essential for the maintenance of specific protein synthesis by this epithelium in vivo.
the synthesis of specific proteins in isolated seminal-vesicle epithelial cells is androgen dependent and is not affected by castration-induced changes in the general protein-synthesis machinery.

the synthesis and secretion of specific proteins by isolated epithelism of guinea-pigs seminal vesicles.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
castration leads to a decrease of specific protein synthesis in the epithelium of the guinea-pig vesicula seminalis, which is reversed by androgen replacement.
the androgenic control of protein synthesis in guinea-pig epithelium is mediated by androgens, not by 3alpha-androstenediol.
the synthesis of specific proteins in isolated epithelum is regulated by androgens.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
castration leads to a decrease both in the amount of specific protein and the capability of the epithelism to synthesize these proteins in vitro.
castration leads to a reduction in specific protein synthesis and in cytoplasmic proteins.
castration leads to a decrease of general and specific protein synthesis and that androgen replacement restores general and specific protein-synthesizing capability to approx. 60% of control values.
The main takeaway from our work is that

androgen deprivation leads not only to a decrease in epithelial weight and cytoplamic protein content, but also to a decrease in the capability of isolated epithelium to synthesize specific protein in vitro.
the seminal vesicle epithelium of the guinea pig is a useful system for investigating the mechanisms of action of testosterone and its metabolites on protein synthesis.

castration of the male guinea pig results in a decrease of specific protein synthesis in vivo and in vitro, and that androgen replacement therapy can restore specific protein synthesis in the seminal vesicle to near-normal values.
